rows.description: A child who takes a classmate's pencil case says they are just borrowing it, or calls cruel teasing a joke; softer words make the act feel less harmful and less of a personal choice.
A teenager labels repeated nasty comments about a peer as banter and says everyone jokes like that; the label hides how the target feels.

rows.subtype: Wants warm, sweet, soft things now [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler seeks sweets, cuddles and bubbles and cries when they stop; seeking pleasure and comfort is a simple, natural drive at this age.

rows.subtype: Lives for fun and good times [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager plans around films, outings and food, and finds long-term duty dull; the love of enjoyment brings vitality and friends, and can crowd out work if it rules everything.

rows.subtype: Pleasure versus duty in the hostel [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult skips a study session for a late-night outing and enjoys it fully while feeling a pinch of guilt; enjoyment and responsibility pull in different directions.
A toddler is guided by a parent to fold hands or bend toward a grandparent's feet and does it as a game. The child feels the smiles and blessing in return and links the gesture to warmth.
A teenager asks whether touching feet is real respect or habit and sometimes does it hurriedly. Doing it with attention to the person makes it real; doing it for show empties it.
A young adult chooses between touching feet, a handshake or a namaste depending on age, gender, faith and comfort of the person. Reading the other person's cue is more polite than one fixed rule.

Adults teach young children that bodies are private, that no adult should ask for secrets from parents, and that they can always tell a trusted grown-up. Simple repeated rules protect better than fear.

A parent or teacher who hears a child mention a secret, gifts or pressure stays calm, thanks the child for telling, believes them and acts to protect. Reactions of anger at the child can stop future telling.
A student makes a joke or a compliment based on a group stereotype, sincerely thinking it is friendly. They are shocked to learn it hurt, because the intent was kind but the effect was not.

rows.subtype: Being told about an unintended slight [Actor]
rows.description: A person is quietly told that their comment came across badly. They feel defensive, embarrassed and misjudged, and do better by listening, apologising for the effect and adjusting without demanding comfort.
A teenager whose speech races when anxious can practise measured pace by pausing at full stops and breathing out first. A steadier pace often helps the speaker feel calmer as well as sound calmer.

rows.subtype: Measured pace in interviews and presentations [Regulating]
rows.description: A young adult in an interview or seminar who keeps a measured pace with deliberate pauses appears organized. Slowing too much may read as disinterest, so pace should fit the room and topic.

rows.subtype: Measured voice in delivering hard news [Regulating]
rows.description: A young manager or clinician delivering bad news uses a slow, measured pace and clear sentences so the listener can take it in. Rushing through it to end the discomfort tends to sound cold.
